name: Rendezvous

origin.note: Deterministic rendezvous of labelled agents in arbitrary graphs was posed by Dessmark, Fraigniaud and Pelc at ESA 2003. Rendezvous itself is older (randomized search games); the catalogue covers the deterministic line [Pelc2019Survey].

derived_from.relation: If the agents can break symmetry (for example by their labels), one may wait while the other explores, so exploration solves rendezvous; the work is in doing better than that, or in meeting when neither knows who should wait [Pelc2019Survey].

summary: Two agents start at different nodes of an unknown graph and must meet; how long does it take, and how much memory or symmetry breaking does it need?
statement: Two mobile agents start at different nodes of an unknown connected port-labelled graph. In the synchronous model they must be at the same node in the same round; in the asynchronous model an adversary controls their speeds and they may also meet inside an edge. Agents are either **labelled** (distinct labels from $\{1,\dots,L\}$; $\lambda$ is the smaller label) or **anonymous**. They may start at different times; $\tau$ is the delay. **Time** is the number of rounds from the start of the later agent (synchronous) or the total number of edge traversals (asynchronous cost). **Memory** is bits per agent.

primer.intro: Two friends lose each other in a city with no phones and want to meet at the same spot. Two agents start at different nodes of an unknown connected graph (dots joined by lines) with port numbers on the edges (local numbers of the edges at each node). Time passes in synchronous **rounds**; in each round an agent stays or walks along one edge, and the agents meet when they are on the same node in the same round (crossing inside an edge does not count). In the basic version each agent knows its own **label**, a distinct integer from $\{1,\dots,L\}$, but not the other's label and nothing about the graph; $\lambda$ is the smaller of the two labels, $n$ the number of nodes, and the later agent may start $\tau$ rounds after the earlier one. The task is to meet, and the cost is the number of rounds from the start of the later agent.

ideas.title: Explore or wait, bit by bit (trees, simultaneous start)
ideas.idea:
If one agent knew it should wait, the other could simply search the graph ("wait for mommy" in [Dessmark2006Deterministic]). Without knowing the other label, use the bits of your own label to take turns. This is a simplified version of their idea, for a tree (no cycles), both agents starting in the same round.
1. Explore the tree by depth-first search and return to your start node; you learn $n$, and this takes $2(n-1)$ rounds. Call $2(n-1)$ rounds a **block**.
2. Write your label in binary, write every bit twice, and append $0\,1$. For example $5 = 101$ becomes $11\,00\,11\,01$.
3. Go through this string one bit per block: on a bit 1, explore the tree and return to your start node; on a bit 0, wait at your start node for the whole block.
ideas.analysis: Both agents compute the same block length, so their blocks line up. Two different labels give strings that differ at some position before the shorter one ends (the final $0\,1$ marks the end, and no doubled bit looks like it). In that block one agent explores while the other waits at its start node, so the explorer walks onto it. The cost is $O(\log\lambda)$ blocks of $O(n)$ rounds, $O(n\log\lambda)$ in all. [Dessmark2006Deterministic] reach $O(n+\log\lambda)$ on trees even with a delay $\tau$, which is optimal; on general graphs the best known is $\tilde O(n^5\log\lambda)$ [TaShma2014Deterministic], against a lower bound of $\Omega(n^2)$.
ideas.why_it_matters: Turning distinct labels into different move/wait patterns is the basic symmetry-breaking device of deterministic rendezvous.

ideas.title: Identical agents in symmetric positions
ideas.idea: Take a ring of 6 nodes where at every node port 0 leads clockwise and port 1 counterclockwise. Put two agents without labels (**anonymous**: same algorithm, same initial memory) on opposite nodes, 3 edges apart, starting in the same round. Each agent sees exactly what the other sees: a node of degree 2, the same entry ports, nobody else around. So in every round they make the same choice: both stay, both go clockwise, or both go counterclockwise.
ideas.analysis: After any number of rounds they are still exactly 3 edges apart, so they never meet, whatever the algorithm and however much memory they have. Identical agents can meet only when their starting positions are not symmetric in this sense, and for those positions $\Theta(\log n)$ bits of memory are exactly what is needed [Czyzowicz2012Forget].
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why most rendezvous work gives the agents labels, and why for identical agents the question becomes which starting positions can be told apart.

ideas.title: Two nodes and the length of a label
ideas.idea: Take the smallest graph: two nodes joined by one edge, one agent at each end, both starting together. Until they meet, an agent sees nothing new (always degree 1, always port 0), so its behaviour in the first $t$ rounds is a string of $t$ choices, stay or move, fixed by its label alone. They meet in a round where exactly one of them moves; if both move they just swap ends.
ideas.analysis: There are only $2^t$ strings of $t$ choices. Among $2^t + 1$ labels, two give the same string; give these labels to the two agents and they do the same thing in each of the first $t$ rounds, so they do not meet within $t$ rounds. Hence some pairs of labels need about $\log$ (number of labels) rounds, which gives the $\Omega(\log\lambda)$ bound of [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. Together with the $\Omega(n)$ needed to cover the graph it shows their $O(n+\log\lambda)$ algorithm for trees is optimal.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that the cost of breaking symmetry is the length of a label, a counting argument that recurs in every model with identifiers.

history: Deterministic rendezvous in graphs started with the question of **feasibility and cost polynomial in the graph size and the label length**, for labelled agents that may start at different times [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. The community then removed the dependence on the delay [Kowalski2008Meet], made the algorithms constructive [TaShma2014Deterministic], asked how little **memory** anonymous agents need [Czyzowicz2012Forget] [Fraigniaud2013Delays], and moved to asynchronous agents, where even feasibility in every graph took years [DeMarco2006Asynchronous] [Czyzowicz2012Everywhere] [Dieudonne2015Polynomial]. Pelc's survey records this evolution [Pelc2019Survey].

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds after the later agent starts (synchronous); edge traversals (asynchronous)

axes.name: Graph size

values.label: finite or countably infinite, degrees may be infinite
values.definition: $G$ is finite or countably infinite; degrees may be infinite.

values.label: finite or countably infinite, every degree finite
values.definition: $G$ is finite or countably infinite with finite degrees.

axes.origin: Deterministic rendezvous in graphs was posed for finite graphs, where an agent can afford to explore the whole graph and the cost is a function of $n$ [Dessmark2006Deterministic] [Pelc2019Survey]. Bhagat and Pelc argued that this approach "is inefficient for very large graphs, and cannot be used for infinite graphs", and gave the first synchronous algorithm for connected graphs with finite degrees and finitely or countably many nodes, with time polynomial in $d$, $\log L$ and the number of paths of length $d$ from the starting nodes, a quantity that also bounds rendezvous from below in trees [Bhagat2022Meet]. For asynchronous agents, Czyzowicz, Labourel and Pelc had already shown that rendezvous is feasible in every connected countable graph [Czyzowicz2012Everywhere] (as summarised in [Pelc2019Survey]); like all earlier work it assumed finite degrees [Pattanayak2024Treasure]. Pattanayak and Pelc then allowed countably infinite degrees, where the path count is infinite, and obtained a universal synchronous algorithm with time polynomial in a weight of the path types between the starting nodes and in $\log L$, matched up to a polynomial by a lower bound in the tree whose degrees are all infinite [Pattanayak2024Treasure]. The axis thus separates three cost measures: $n$, the local path count, and path-type weights.

axes.name: Start

values.label: arbitrary delay between the two starts
values.definition: An adversary wakes the agents at times $t_1$ and $t_2$; the delay $\tau=|t_1-t_2|$ is unknown.

values.label: simultaneous start
values.definition: Both agents start in the same round ($\tau=0$).

axes.origin:
Dessmark, Fraigniaud, Kowalski and Pelc treated two startup scenarios for deterministic rendezvous: simultaneous startup, and an arbitrary delay $	au$ chosen by the adversary, in which each agent counts rounds from its own wake-up without knowing $	au$ [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. The delay is the stronger adversary: it can delay one agent long enough that the other must find it while it sleeps, which is treasure hunt [Pelc2019Survey] [TaShma2014Deterministic]. It changes cost: on a ring simultaneous start gives $\Theta(d\log \lambda)$, while with arbitrary delay $\Omega(n+d\log \lambda)$ is a lower bound even when $n$ is known; and the first polynomial algorithm for arbitrary graphs had cost growing with $\sqrt	au$, leaving open whether the dependence could be removed [Dessmark2006Deterministic], which Kowalski and Malinowski and then Ta-Shma and Zwick did [Kowalski2008Meet] [TaShma2014Deterministic] (the first as summarised in [Pelc2019Survey]). It also changes memory: Fraigniaud and Pelc showed that identical agents need $\Theta(\log n)$ bits in trees with arbitrary delay, even on a line, but only $O(\log
u+\log\log n)$ bits with simultaneous start in trees with $
u$ leaves, an exponential gap when $
u$ is small [Fraigniaud2013Delays].

variants.title: Labelled agents, arbitrary finite graphs
variants.summary: Polynomial in $n$ and $\log \lambda$ and independent of the delay, but far from the known lower bounds.

preconditions: Theorem 4.4: for all $n$ and all pairs of labels, a regular graph made of two cliques of $n/2$ nodes joined by two swapped edges, ports equal at both ends of each edge
the two-node graph, agents at both ends, simultaneous start: with fewer steps than label bits two labels produce the same move/stay sequence

results.note: Theorem 4.3: polynomial in $n$, $\tau$ and $\log\lambda$. Not constructive in the computational sense: each agent finds, by exhaustive local search, a combinatorial object whose existence is proved by the probabilistic method; only moves are counted.
First bound independent of $\tau$ (as stated in [Pelc2019Survey]); needs backtracking (as stated in [TaShma2014Deterministic]).
assumes: backtracking: the agent learns the port by which it entered

results.note: Independent of $\tau$ and needs no backtracking, but not explicit: it relies on universal traversal sequences that are only known to exist. Checked in the paper. ([Xin2007Faster] wrongly says it uses backtracking.)

memory.note: Memory is unbounded in these algorithms.

open: Find an optimal-time synchronous rendezvous algorithm for labelled agents in arbitrary graphs (open problem of [Pelc2019Survey]).
variants.notes: $\ell$ in [TaShma2014Deterministic] is the length of the shorter label, our $\log \lambda$. Checked against the full text of [Dessmark2006Deterministic]: there agents know only their own label, learn the entry port and the degree at each node, and do not notice crossing inside an edge. With **simultaneous** start the same paper meets in $O(d\Delta^{d}\log\lambda)$ rounds in any graph without knowing $\Delta$ (Theorem 4.1), optimal when $d$ and $\Delta$ are bounded. **Unverified against the original paper:** the bound of [Kowalski2008Meet] (from [Pelc2019Survey]); [TaShma2014Deterministic] was read in full.

variants.title: Labelled agents in trees
variants.summary: In trees, $O(n+\log \lambda)$ even with arbitrary delay, and this cannot be improved.

preconditions: Theorem 2.3: two stars of $n/2-1$ leaves whose centres are joined, agents at the centres, for the $\Omega(n)$ part; the two-node argument for the $\Omega(\log\lambda)$ part

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2.2), with arbitrary delay: explore by depth-first search, go to the central node or the central edge, and on a central edge run Procedure Extend-Labels, which meets on $K_2$ within $2\log\lambda+6$ rounds.
assumes: agents know that the graph is a tree, but not its size

variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Dessmark2006Deterministic].

variants.title: Labelled agents in rings, simultaneous start
variants.summary: With simultaneous start on a ring, rendezvous takes $\Theta(d\log \lambda)$ for initial distance $d$.

preconditions: agents know that the graph is a ring

results.note: Introductory and current best (Lemmas 3.1, 3.2 and Theorem 3.1).
assumes: agents know that the graph is a ring, but not its size

variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. With **arbitrary delay** on an $n$-node ring, $\Omega(n+d\log\lambda)$ rounds are necessary even when $n$ is known (Proposition 3.1); $O(n\log\lambda)$ suffices for known $n$ (Theorem 3.2) and $O(\lambda\tau+\lambda n^2)$ for unknown $n$ (Theorem 3.3) [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. The paper announces that a forthcoming paper reaches $O(n\log\lambda)$ with arbitrary delay; as stated in [Pelc2019Survey], this is [Kowalski2008Meet], for unknown $n$.

variants.title: Labelled agents, graphs with infinite degrees
variants.summary: A universal algorithm works even when nodes have infinite degree; it is within a cubic factor of the lower bound.

preconditions: $W=\max(w(v_1,v_2),w(v_2,v_1))$, the path weight of the treasure-hunt variant
e.g. the infinite tree with all degrees infinite

open: Find an optimal rendezvous algorithm, "even for finite graphs" [Pattanayak2024Treasure].

variants.title: Anonymous agents: memory
variants.summary: Identical agents can meet whenever their positions are not symmetric, and $\Theta(\log n)$ bits are exactly what it takes.

results.note: Introductory and current best; any delay; also gives the first polynomial-time computation of a quotient graph.

variants.notes: Rendezvous is feasible exactly when the two starting nodes have different views.

variants.title: Anonymous agents in trees, simultaneous start
variants.summary: With simultaneous start, memory drops to $\Theta(\log \nu+\log\log n)$ for trees with $\nu$ leaves; with delay it is $\Theta(\log n)$, an exponential gap.

results.note: Introductory and current best. With arbitrary delay, $\Omega(\log n)$ even on lines.

variants.title: Asynchronous labelled agents
variants.summary: An adversary controls speeds; agents may meet inside an edge. Feasible everywhere, and at polynomial cost, but with very large exponents.

assumes: an upper bound on the size is known
results.note: On a ring of known size, cost $O(n\log \lambda)$, which is optimal.
Feasible in every connected countable graph without any knowledge; cost at least exponential.

time.note: No lower bound recorded for general graphs.

open: Find an optimal-cost asynchronous rendezvous algorithm in arbitrary graphs (open problem of [Pelc2019Survey]).

variants.title: Asynchronous anonymous agents
variants.summary: Which pairs of starting nodes allow identical asynchronous agents to meet is characterised.

results.note: Introductory and current best. Feasible iff the views differ or the two nodes are joined by a path whose port sequence is a palindrome (as summarised in [Pelc2019Survey]); randomized agents meet with probability 1.

figure.caption: Rendezvous of two labelled agents in a tree, simultaneous start, by the explore-or-wait idea of [Dessmark2006Deterministic] (simplified): after one depth-first tour to learn $n$, each agent reads its label in binary with every bit doubled and $01$ appended, and spends one block of $2(n-1)$ rounds per bit, exploring and returning on a 1, waiting at home on a 0. Labels 1 and 3 give $11\,01$ and $11\,11\,01$; in block 3 agent 3 explores while agent 1 waits, and they meet. One frame per round.

frames.label: Start: agents 1 and 3 at the ends of a tree (n = 4)
Block 0: both explore; they learn n (block = 6 rounds)
Block 3: bits 0 and 1; agent 1 waits, agent 3 explores
Final: agent 3 walks onto the waiting agent 1 in round 21
